RAUC runs the system pre-install handler before any slot is written and marks the new slot active (r_mark_active, inside the default install handler) before it runs the post-install handler; this order is the same in v1.13 (Debian 13) and current master. RAUC system handlers receive RAUC_BUNDLE_MOUNT_POINT, RAUC_TARGET_SLOTS and RAUC_SLOT_BOOTNAME_<N>; RAUC_MF_VERSION is documented only for install hooks, so a handler must read the version from the mounted bundle's manifest.

RAUC's GRUB backend treats a slot as good only when it is in ORDER with _OK=1 and _TRY=0, and mark-good writes _OK=1,_TRY=0; combined with Home Assistant OS's GRUB script (try while TRY<3, increment every boot) this gives exactly 3 boot attempts per unconfirmed slot. Observed in the lab: A_TRY went 1,2,3 then GRUB chose the other slot.

RAUC's GRUB backend implements mark-good as <slot>_OK=1,<slot>_TRY=0 and mark-bad as <slot>_OK=0,<slot>_TRY=0 in grubenv.
RAUC's GRUB backend activates a slot by setting <slot>_OK=1, <slot>_TRY=0 and putting it first in ORDER.
RAUC's reference GRUB script boots the first slot in ORDER with OK=1 and TRY=0, then sets its TRY=1 before booting, so an uncommitted slot gets exactly one boot attempt.
RAUC docs say the grubenv must live outside the redundant rootfs partitions, e.g. /EFI/BOOT/grubenv on the EFI partition, with load_env/save_env --file in grub.cfg.

RAUC's efi bootloader backend marks a newly installed slot primary by setting the one-shot EFI BootNext variable (efi-use-bootnext defaults to true); mark-good prepends the slot to BootOrder, mark-bad removes it from BootOrder, and a slot counts as good only while it is listed in BootOrder.

RAUC determines the booted slot from an explicit rauc.slot=<bootname> on the kernel command line before other methods, so a UKI whose signed command line carries rauc.slot= identifies its slot even when booted from a fallback loader path.

EDK II's boot manager (edk2-stable202502, the base of Debian 13's OVMF 2025.02) deletes the BootNext variable before transferring control to that boot option and then walks BootOrder, so a BootNext target that fails to load or start is tried only once per power-on.

claim: PCR 7 (secure-boot-policy) records the Secure Boot state and changes when Secure Boot is enabled/disabled or the firmware certificates (PK, KEK, db, dbx) change; systemd-cryptenroll binds to PCR 7 only by default.

systemd-cryptenroll --tpm2-public-key= / --tpm2-public-key-pcrs= / --tpm2-signature= binds a LUKS2 key to a signed PCR policy, so any PCR values signed by the key holder unlock it (survives kernel updates) instead of one fixed set of PCR values.

systemd-pcrphase extends PCR 11 with boot-phase strings (enter-initrd, leave-initrd, sysinit, ready, …); enter-initrd/leave-initrd are measured by systemd-pcrphase-initrd.service, which only runs in a systemd-based initrd.

Kopia supports S3 Object Lock in COMPLIANCE mode set at repository creation (--retention-mode COMPLIANCE --retention-period) and can renew the locks during full maintenance (kopia maintenance set --extend-object-locks true; full-interval must be at least 1 day shorter than the retention period); Azure (version-level immutability) and Google (object retention) are supported the same way; point-in-time reconnect (--point-in-time) is S3 only

restic does not set or extend object-lock retention itself: the 0.13.0 change only added upload checksums so that restic 'can now be used to store backups in S3 buckets which have Object Lock enabled'; issue #5041 (open since 2024-09-02) lists the drawbacks of restic's append-only model, which needs a separate trusted host for forget/prune

Kopia Repository Server: clients authenticate with a per-user username@hostname password and proxy all access through the server without storage credentials; each user sees only its own snapshot and policy manifests; ACLs configurable with 'kopia server acl' since v0.8; caveat: only manifests are access-controlled, not contents

restic design doc: an adversary with a leaked decrypted key can decrypt existing and future data of every host in the repository, and 'a password change will not prevent this'; changing the master key needs 'copy' into a new repository; so removing one of restic's multiple keys does not revoke a leaked key

Kopia uses envelope encryption: the repository password derives a key (scrypt-65536-8-1) that encrypts the format blob holding the content keys; ChangePassword re-derives the format key and rewrites only the repository config and blobcfg blobs, not the data

Kopia's committed content index cache is memory-mapped from disk (mmapFile then index.Open) rather than loaded into the heap; the caching doc describes the indexes cache as 'a format that can be directly memory-mapped'

Kopia Actions (since v0.8): opt-in before/after commands per snapshot root and per folder, for database dumps, filesystem snapshots (e.g. ZFS) and notifications; an action can redirect the upload to another directory such as a snapshot mountpoint

Kopia 'repository sync-to' (since v0.6) incrementally replicates a whole repository to another storage location without re-encryption; deletions in the target are off unless --delete; --must-exist guards against an unmounted target
Kopia full maintenance runs 'kopia snapshot verify' daily (CLI and KopiaUI); --verify-files-percent downloads and decrypts a random sample, the equivalent of a partial test restore
Kopia states that large clock skew between clients and storage 'can lead to major inconsistencies, including Kopia deleting its own data'; only a few minutes of skew are tolerated

Kopia compatibility promise: each version reads snapshots from the current and at least one previous minor version (for v0.x); reading older formats is 'likely' but not guaranteed; format upgrades need explicit human action
Kopia's Reed-Solomon error correction must be chosen at repository creation and is marked 'currently experimental. Use at your own risk'

The balenaOS disk image has five partitions: boot (resin-boot), root A, root B, state (resin-state) and data (resin-data)
Default sizes: boot 100 MiB, state 80 MiB; each root slot is sized from a fixed 1460 MiB image budget minus boot and state, divided by two (~640 MiB per slot by default)
The root filesystem is built by Yocto, imported as a Docker image (docker import/save), then written with mkfs.hostapp into a hostapp-ext4 root partition: the OS itself is a container image

Image and EFI/RSA signing at build time is done by calling a remote signing service (SIGN_API with an API key header), so private keys are not on the build host; a signed build produces a balenaos-img.sig

The host OS update client (hostapp-update) pulls the new OS as a container image with balenaEngine (or loads a local tarball), creates it in the inactive sysroot and atomically switches the 'current' symlink there
Before updating, hostapp-update records whether the VPN (cloud link) was online, for the post-update health check
hostapp-update first deletes every container, image and hostapp in the inactive sysroot, so the previous-previous OS is gone before the new one is written
Docs: the updater tries a delta first, then a full pull from balenaCloud's registry, and falls back to Docker Hub if both fail
During an update the 80-rollback hook writes rollback-health and rollback-altboot breadcrumb files to the state partition
rollback-health waits 60 s after boot, then retries the health tests every 60 s up to 15 times; on failure it runs the previous OS's hooks from the inactive root and reboots into it
When tests pass, rollback-health commits: balena-extension-manager hup commit, rollback-stop, then commit hooks

The health tests check only (a) the VPN reconnects if it was online before the update, (b) the balenaEngine healthcheck and (c) an optional board-specific script; the Supervisor and user apps are not checked
rollback-altboot: the bootloader counts boots when upgrade_available=1 and boots the previous root if the count exceeds 1, i.e. the new OS never reached userspace
Docs: once a host OS update succeeds, there is no rollback to the previous OS version except the automatic rollbacks
Docs: since Q3 2026 OS updates are queued; the Supervisor fetches the request, retries twice, then every two days; offline devices update when they reconnect
The Supervisor refuses app updates and reboots while rollback breadcrumbs exist, so it cannot interrupt a host OS update on trial
On a UEFI device in Secure Boot user mode, the 0-signed-update hook aborts an update to an OS whose boot files are unsigned
The UEFI db is updated during the update, but the dbx (revocation list) update is deferred until rollback-health confirms the new OS
On TPM devices the update re-seals the disk-encryption passphrase to PCRs 0,2,3,7 including the new GRUB and kernel hashes
Docs: Secure Boot images are pre-signed with balena-owned keys (no Microsoft shim by default); customer keys are a paid extra service
Docs: the chain of trust ends at the kernel; the root filesystem is not signed or verified at runtime and integrity relies on disk encryption
Docs: application container images are not cryptographically signed; integrity relies on TLS to balenaCloud and digest-pinned pulls
Docs: Secure Boot and full-disk encryption are only offered together, through installer images; memory-constrained devices cannot support it

The runtime is one Docker Compose project: Command Center admin (GHCR image, :latest, pull_policy always), MySQL 8.0, Redis 7, Dozzle, an updater sidecar and a disk-collector; the admin container mounts /var/run/docker.sock and drives the host Docker daemon
The admin image is a multi-stage build on node:22-slim (AdonisJS app built with node ace build); the go-pmtiles binary is pinned by version and per-architecture SHA-256

The primary image is built only by a manual workflow_dispatch job gated on an authorised-user list; it pushes :X.Y.Z, :vX.Y.Z and optionally :latest to GHCR; the workflow has no signing, attestation, SBOM or platforms (multi-arch) step
Versions are cut by semantic-release from main, with an rc prerelease branch; the release job is also manual and authorisation-gated

The installer requires /etc/debian_version, warns and continues after 10 seconds on non-x86_64 (ARM tracked in PR #419), installs Docker with get.docker.com, and installs and configures the NVIDIA Container Toolkit when an NVIDIA GPU is detected
The installer downloads compose.yml and the start/stop/update helper scripts from refs/heads/main (not a release tag) with curl and no checksum or signature check
The installer generates the app key and database passwords locally (32 random alphanumerics from /dev/urandom) and writes them into compose.yml with sed

Official install guide: Ubuntu 26.04 LTS recommended, Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian 12 supported; Raspberry Pi/ARM not supported; VMs not officially supported; macOS not supported; WSL2 community-supported; focus is x86 bare metal

Hardware guide: runs on any x86 Linux computer; three recommended build tiers ($150-$300, $500-$800, $1000+); product links are affiliate links that fund development; Raspberry Pi users are pointed to Internet-in-a-Box

Minimum specs: 2 GHz dual-core, 4 GB RAM (stack without AI under 1 GB), 5 GB disk; optimal: Ryzen 7/Core i7, 32 GB RAM, RTX 3060-class GPU, 250 GB SSD; adding the AI assistant brings the install to about 25 GB

Core update from the UI: the admin writes an update-request file to a shared volume; the sidecar polls every second, rewrites the admin image tag in compose.yml with sed, pulls, then for admin, mysql, redis and dozzle runs stop, rm and up; on any failure it writes status error and returns, with no step that restores the previous image or tag
The CLI update script runs docker compose pull then up -d --force-recreate for the core stack, with no rollback

Core auto-update is opt-in (default off), runs in a 02:00-05:00 window after a 72-hour cool-off, takes only same-major strict-semver non-prerelease releases from the GitHub releases API, and disables itself after 3 consecutive failures
No update path (auto_update_service, system_update_service, sidecar) verifies an image signature or pins a digest; the target is a tag name and trust rests on GHCR and the GitHub releases feed

App (service) updates rename the live container to <name>_old, create the new one from the inspected config, wait 5 seconds and require it to be Running (the recreate path polls a declared HEALTHCHECK up to 30 s), and on failure rename the old container back and start it

Issue #949: an app update stopped the old Ollama container and never started the new one, leaving the service gone with the DB unchanged; maintainers fixed it in v1.33.0 by adding rollback to the previous container

There is no app manifest file: each app is a row in a services DB table seeded from a TypeScript array compiled into the admin image, holding the image, a Docker Engine API container_config JSON (binds, ports, env), ui_location, category and depends_on

The v1.35.1 catalog seeds 17 services (Kiwix, Qdrant, Ollama, CyberChef, FlatNotes, Kolibri, Stirling-PDF, FileBrowser, Calibre-Web, IT-Tools, Excalidraw, Meshtastic Web, MeshCore Web, Homebox, Vaultwarden, Jellyfin, nomad-translate), mostly pinned by version tag; FileBrowser uses the floating v2 tag

User-defined custom containers are allowed behind a guard that hard-blocks bind mounts of the Docker socket, /etc, /proc, /sys, /boot, /dev, /run, /var/run and the NOMAD install tree, and only warns on registries outside docker.io, ghcr.io, lscr.io and quay.io
There is no authentication: the router middleware stack has the session middleware commented out and the named-middleware set is empty; the README states NOMAD includes no authentication by design
CSRF protection is disabled in the Shield config (enabled: false with a TODO)
Container-creating routes (/api/system/services/install, /uninstall, /custom create/update/delete) are registered with no route-level middleware

Security policy: only the latest release gets security fixes; no authentication, attacks needing LAN access, and anything needing internet exposure are out of scope; the local network is the trust boundary; small team with no guaranteed response time
The benchmark-submission HMAC key is a constant in source and therefore in the public image (value not reproduced here); SECURITY.md accepts this and relies on leaderboard moderation
The Creator Packs entitlement key is injected into official image builds from a CI secret and baked into an ENV layer; the Dockerfile comment accepts that it is extractable from the public image

Proxmox VE 9.0 released 2025-08-05 on Debian 13 trixie; 9.1 on 2025-11-19 (Debian 13.2); 9.2 on 2026-05-21 (Debian 13.5, kernel 7.0 default, QEMU 11.0, LXC 7.0, ZFS 2.4)
The current development state analysed is pve-manager 9.2.27, proxmox-installer 9.2.9, pve-container 6.1.20 and proxmox-kernel-helper 9.2.1 (all 'trixie' in debian/changelog)

Proxmox VE versions are supported at least as long as the matching Debian release has Debian Security support (about 3 years); PVE 8 (Debian 12, first release 2023-06) reached EOL 2026-08; PVE 9 EOL is 'tba'; Proxmox calls this a rolling release model
Proxmox VE code is licensed AGPL-3.0 (FAQ); pve-manager, pve-container and pve-access-control debian/copyright declare AGPL-3+
proxmox-kernel-helper (proxmox-boot-tool) is GPL-2.0 only ('version 2 dated June, 1991'); pve-docs is GFDL-1.3-no-invariants-or-later
The installer does not build the OS: it unpacks a prebuilt '<product>-base.squashfs' from the ISO with unsquashfs into /target

After the squashfs, the installer dpkg-unpacks every .deb shipped under proxmox/packages/ on the ISO (skipping bootloader, Secure Boot and microcode packages that do not fit the hardware) and then runs dpkg --configure -a
The tool that builds the base squashfs and the ISO is not in Proxmox's public git: git.proxmox.com's project index lists pve-installer, dab and proxmox-kernel-helper but no ISO-build repository
Disk layout: GPT with a 1 MB BIOS-boot partition (x86 only), an ESP of 1024 MB on disks over 100 GB (else 512 MB) and one OS partition; hard minimum 2 GB, warning below 8 GB
With ext4/xfs the OS partition becomes an LVM VG 'pve' with swap, one root LV (capped at 96 GiB by default) and a 'data' thin pool for guests; there is no second root slot
ZFS and Btrfs roots are also offered by the installer (ZFS root at rpool/ROOT/<volume>); with Secure Boot the ESP is set up by proxmox-boot-tool in 'grub' mode
On arm64 no signed shim exists yet, so the installer falls back to the plain GRUB EFI image as the removable-media loader (i.e. no Secure Boot chain on arm64)

Updates are plain apt: pveupgrade is 'a small wrapper around apt-get dist-upgrade' that refuses if the package cache is older than 3 days and only prints 'please consider rebooting' after a kernel update
Point releases are upgraded with 'apt update; apt full-upgrade' from the web UI or CLI; major upgrades are supported in place but must be 'carefully planned and tested'
The only OS-level rollback is the kernel: proxmox-boot-tool 'kernel pin <ver> [--next-boot]' sets the default or next-boot kernel among those still in /boot
apt auto-removal keeps the running kernel, the two latest, the latest of each older series and the pinned kernel, so a fallback kernel is always installed
Major upgrades ship a checker (pve8to9, 2,408 lines, ~30 check_* functions); its bootloader check warns that an unmounted ESP or missing grub-efi-amd64 'may leave the system unbootable'

The 8-to-9 guide offers two paths: new install plus restore of guests from backup, or in-place apt upgrade (sed bookworm->trixie in sources, run pve8to9); a 'valid and tested backup is always required'

Real failure: after an 8-to-9 upgrade a host dropped to a grub> prompt (old GRUB in firmware NVRAM / ESP); recovery needed a manual kernel boot and grub-install, and one user saw it return after full power loss
Real failure: a user who removed systemd-boot during the 8-to-9 upgrade got a GRUB reboot loop; the 9.1 ISO rescue boot could not find /boot/pve/vmlinuz
Real failure (9 beta): a fresh 8-to-9 upgrade in a VM no longer booted; a Proxmox reply attributes it to a missing proxmox-boot-tool reinit when the grub/shim update arrived
App/template catalogue: pveam downloads aplinfo.dat plus a detached .asc signature and verifies it with sqv against /usr/share/doc/pve-manager/trustedkeys.gpg before use
Template downloads require a hash (hash_required => 1) checked against the sha512sum/md5sum from the signed index; only types 'lxc' and 'openvz' are accepted

OCI images become LXC containers: an archive with oci-layout, index.json and blobs/ is extracted inside the container's user namespace, and Entrypoint/Cmd, User, WorkingDir, Env and StopSignal are mapped into the LXC config (Volumes only become empty directories)
PVE 9.1 added creating LXC containers from OCI images (upload or registry pull); application containers from OCI are a technology preview

Roadmap (planned, not shipped): mature OCI support and declarative multi-guest apps based on the Compose Specification; native LUKS full-disk encryption of the root in the installer; a system-wide health-check framework
Community-scripts/ProxmoxVE (MIT, ~30k stars, 652 ct/ scripts at c1e45c1c) is the de facto one-command app catalogue for PVE; it is a third-party project, not Proxmox's
Cluster config lives in pmxcfs, a database-driven file system (SQLite) replicated to all nodes by Corosync, size-limited to 128 MiB, mounted at /etc/pve
HA needs at least three nodes for reliable quorum (QDevice for 2-node); HA fencing uses a hardware watchdog or falls back to the kernel softdog
Backups: vzdump has stop, suspend and snapshot modes plus backup fleecing; with Proxmox Backup Server, backups can be client-side encrypted with AES-256-GCM and the key wrapped by an RSA master key

Identity: realms are Linux PAM, the built-in PVE server, LDAP, Microsoft AD and OpenID Connect (src/PVE/Auth/{PAM,PVE,LDAP,AD,OpenId}.pm); second factors are TOTP, WebAuthn, YubiKey OTP and recovery keys; roles + ACL paths; API tokens
Secure Boot has been supported out of the box since PVE 8.1 (released 2023-11-23) via a Microsoft-signed shim, Proxmox-signed GRUB and Proxmox-signed kernels; only GRUB is supported

Hardware: x86-64 plus official arm64 since 2026-08 on NVIDIA Grace and Vera; other UEFI+ACPI ARMv9 hardware is best-effort; device-tree-only SBCs such as the Raspberry Pi are not supported; eval minimum 1 GB RAM, recommended 2 GB + guests
Arm64 port was developed with NVIDIA and Supermicro and validated on Grace Hopper; separately Proxmox announced (2026-07-28) a collaboration placing PVE under NVIDIA Mission Control for AI factories
No AI assistant, MCP server or LLM feature appears in the PVE 9.x release notes or roadmap (whole-word search for AI, MCP and LLM in the saved roadmap returned nothing)

Business model: every feature is free; paid per-CPU-socket subscriptions buy the enterprise repository and support: Community EUR 120, Basic EUR 370, Standard EUR 550, Premium EUR 1,100 per socket per year; arm64 keys are separate and arm64 support is 'upon request'

Repositories: pve-enterprise (needs a subscription key, enabled by default, 'most stable'), pve-no-subscription ('testing and non-production use') and pve-test; all signed with proxmox-archive-keyring
Company: Proxmox Server Solutions GmbH, Vienna, founded 2005; subscription model since 2013; self-reported 1.5 million hosts and 200,000+ community members (2025)
Install paths: ISO (graphical and TUI), automated install from an answer file, and install on top of an existing Debian 13; Proxmox warns the Debian route 'presumes' correct prior setup
Proxmox Datacenter Manager (multi-cluster view) reached 1.0 on 2025-12-04 and 1.1 on 2026-05-28; Proxmox Backup Server 4.0 shipped 2025-08-06 and 4.2 on 2026-04-29, all on Debian 13
Firewall: per-datacenter/node/guest rules, security groups and IP sets; a newer nftables-based proxmox-firewall is available

StartOS v0.4.2 was published 2026-11-09; its release tag start-os/v0.4.2 points to commit 175ce3b (committed 2026-11-08). It is the teardown baseline.

The StartOS repo (now Start9Labs/start-technologies, created 2020-11-13) is an MIT-licensed monorepo holding StartOS, StartWRT, StartTunnel, the registry, start-cli and the TypeScript SDK; a few files (OpenWrt overlay, one Intel BIOS blob) are not MIT.
StartOS 0.4.0 (2026) is described by Start9 as a ground-up rewrite, its third after 0.2.0 (2020) and 0.3.0 (2022); backups from earlier versions are incompatible.

StartOS's backend is one Rust library crate (start-core, Tokio/Axum) behind a JSON-RPC API; the UI is Angular + Taiga UI; state lives in Patch-DB (diff-based, pushed to the browser over WebSocket); each service runs in LXC with a Node.js container runtime.
StartOS images are built with Debian live-build inside a container; the default Debian suite is trixie (Debian 13).

StartOS build targets are x86_64, aarch64 and riscv64 (each standard 'nonfree' and FOSS-only 'slim'), x86_64-nvidia, aarch64-nvidia, raspberrypi and rockchip64; Pi and Rockchip ship as .img, everything else as hybrid ISO installers. There is no Jetson/L4T target.

The Raspberry Pi image pins Raspberry Pi's vendor kernel 6.18.33+rpt with flavours rpi-v8 and rpi-2712 (the Pi 5 kernel flavour), yet the docs say StartOS 0.4.x supports the Raspberry Pi 4 ONLY, and a Pi must be reflashed for a major version upgrade (no over-the-air path).

On x86_64 and arm64 StartOS pins linux-image, linux-headers and NVIDIA packages to Debian trixie-backports (priority 500), so it ships a backports kernel rather than trixie's stable kernel; shipped images carried 7.0.4+deb13 and 7.2.11+deb13 kernels per issues #3465 and #4647.
Debian says backports 'cannot be tested as extensively as Debian stable' and 'are provided on an as-is basis' ('Use with care!').

StartOS -nvidia images install NVIDIA's .run driver with --kernel-module-type=open inside the image-build chroot and add NVIDIA's container-toolkit apt repo; an earlier build shipped the proprietary module flavour, so Blackwell GPUs (DGX Spark GB10, RTX 50) could not initialise until fixed (issue #3465, closed 2026-07-13).

The Pi/Rockchip .img is GPT with four partitions: 128 MiB firmware (vfat), 100 MB ESP (vfat), 2 GB /boot (vfat) and a btrfs root sized to the squashfs plus 256 MB; the root holds images/<blake3>.rootfs and a config/current.rootfs symlink to it, and GRUB (arm64-efi) boots the Pi.

At boot StartOS's initramfs mounts the squashfs that config/current.rootfs points to (or the newest *.rootfs if the pointer is missing) read-only, layered under a persistent config/overlay and a tmpfs upper layer, so changes outside the overlay vanish on reboot.

A StartOS OS update prunes old images and kernels, downloads the new squashfs to /media/startos/images/next.squashfs, re-verifies its BLAKE3 commitment, extracts and runs the image's own upgrade script, then marks the server 'restart required'.

Before downloading, StartOS requires the registry's OS-update asset to carry a signature from a key the server trusts for StartOS updates; --trust overrides signer trust but not signature or integrity verification.

New StartOS installs trust three signing keys for packages and OS updates (two individual developer keys and a Start9 key); keys are Ed25519 (PEM or GPG); diagnostic-mode updates use PEM keys in /etc/startos/os-signers.

StartOS's upgrade script unpacks the new image's /boot over the single shared /boot partition, runs grub-install and update-grub from a chroot of the new image, signs unsigned kernel modules with the box's own MOK key, then repoints config/current.rootfs at the new image.

StartOS has no boot counter or automatic OS rollback: the initramfs always boots the current.rootfs image, and no code at the tag selects a previous image after a failed boot (searched start-core, build scripts and docs for rollback/bootcount/grubenv/grub-reboot).
Before each OS update StartOS deletes every kernel in /boot except the running one, and deletes the oldest non-current OS images until the new image plus a 1 GiB margin fits.
Start9 documents that StartOS has no automatic OS or service updates (explicit action always required) and that the fallback when a UI update goes wrong is to re-flash.
Start9 warns that an OS update can take up to an hour after restart with no progress shown and the UI unreachable, and tells users not to unplug the server.
If StartOS boots with a database version newer than the running OS, it runs down-migrations (rollback_to_unchecked) on the database, so an older image can run on newer data.
StartOS snapshots a service's data before a service update and restores the snapshot if the update fails; a failed restore is treated as fatal so the old service never starts on new-version data.
Open issue #4454 (2026-10-27): an 'Updating' service entry cannot recover at boot and a failed service rollback has no exit.

S9PK v2 files start with magic bytes 0x3b 0x3b 0x02, are BLAKE3 Merkle archives, and embed an Ed25519 signature with context 's9pk' that readers always verify; extra endorsements go in an optional trailer.

An S9PK holds manifest.json, an icon, LICENSE.md, instructions.md, javascript.squashfs (the package's lifecycle code) and per-architecture container images as squashfs files; the packer rejects archives missing the required files.

The S9PK manifest declares id, Exver version, canMigrateTo/From ranges, images, volumes, dependencies and hardwareRequirements (device filters, RAM, architectures), which the server checks against detected hardware.
StartOS does not use Docker or Podman: each service runs in its own LXC container with namespace-based subcontainers; Start9 says Docker/Podman lacked the reliability and flexibility it needed.

StartOS registries are indexes: the registry lists and signs packages while binaries are hosted anywhere (CDN, GitHub release) and verified on install; StartOS preloads a Start9 Registry (maintained, supported) and a Community Registry (listed only).

StartOS 0.4.1 added an MCP server at /mcp (streamable HTTP) authenticated by a bearer token from 'start-cli auth token create', plus a package.exec API/MCP tool that runs a command in a service's subcontainer.

StartOS's MCP server is opt-out: every API method is exposed as a tool unless its handler sets mcp=false; at v0.4.2 the catalog has 208 tools, including package.exec, package.install/uninstall, server.update, server.shutdown, backup.create, ssh.add and server.update-signers.add.
StartOS bearer tokens are named sessions printed once, revoked manually or after 30 days unused; the docs describe no per-token scopes or per-tool approval.
StartOS has one admin identity (the master password, also usable for SSH); open issue #3881 asks for named, individually revocable dashboard credentials and a read-only tier.

StartOS formats the data drive with LUKS but always unlocks it with a fixed compile-time constant key (DEFAULT_PASSWORD), not a user secret or TPM; Start9's docs state the data drive is not encrypted with the master password 'so anyone holding the server or its drive can read your services' data'; issue #735 (2021) for key-collection UX is still open.

StartOS backs up to a physical drive or a LAN network folder (CIFS), encrypted with the master password; each service is stopped while it is backed up; a backup restores onto other hardware, and onto another CPU architecture under emulation.
StartOS backups use its own FUSE filesystem (startos-backup-fs): append-only segments, ChaCha20 with HMAC-SHA256, and Reed-Solomon erasure coding (default 10 data + 2 parity shards).

StartOS supports UEFI Secure Boot through Debian's shim and a per-box MOK key that signs DKMS/unsigned modules (e.g. NVIDIA) and is re-enrolled at boot if needed; MOK bugs #3702 (closed) and #4499 (open) broke fresh or failed installs.
StartOS root images are squashfs files checked with BLAKE3 at download and before install, but the boot path mounts them without dm-verity or any signature check.

Start9's only server for sale (since Sept 2026) is the Server One (6600H), a rebadged GenMachine Yi6000: AMD Ryzen 5 6600H, 16 or 32 GB soldered LPDDR5, 2 or 4 TB NVMe, 1 GbE, no Wi-Fi, 1-year warranty.
Server One list prices are USD 899 (2 TB/16 GB), 1,099 (2 TB/32 GB), 1,199 (4 TB/16 GB) and 1,399 (4 TB/32 GB).

Start9 sells Premium Support at USD 200/year (a year included with Server One and the router); first-line answers come from 'Dux', an AI support agent, which can hand off to 'Helix', an engineering agent that reads source code and files bug reports.
Start9 Labs raised a USD 1.2M seed round on 2021-03-11 (aggregator data).

Contributor stats at 2026-11-11 show a small core team: the top two human contributors account for 2,167 commits; the third-largest contributor account (329 commits) is an automated agent account, and a docs bot has 150.

Issue #4647 (closed 2026-11-09): an OS update dropped the user's kernel parameters from grub.cfg, because edits to /etc/default/grub live on the tmpfs upper layer and update-grub runs in a chroot of the new image.
Issue #3923 (closed 2026-09-17): the installer wrote kernel device names (e.g. /dev/sdb1) to /etc/fstab, so a re-enumerated disk dropped a server into unrecoverable emergency mode.
Issue #4435 (open): after the 0.3.5.1 → 0.4.0.1 migration, a Start9 server on the FOSS-only image lost Wi-Fi because iwlwifi firmware is not in that image.
Issue #4009 (closed): the Pi image never grew its btrfs root because init_resize.sh resized through a read-only bind mount and ignored the failure.

StartOS moved 0.3.5.1 x86 boxes to the 0.4.0 layout over the air: the old updater staged a payload, and the new initramfs migrates the disk layout on first boot, keeping only the data partition; Pi boxes had to reflash.
StartOS health checks are defined per service by the package developer (Starting/Loading/Success/Error with a grace period); they gate service readiness, not the OS update.
StartOS release images are hosted on a DigitalOcean Spaces CDN; the GitHub release lists SHA-256 checksums and carries a signatures.tar.gz asset.
StartOS ships aarch64-nvidia images aimed at the NVIDIA DGX Spark and adds a boot argument to avoid a GB10 hang (initcall_blacklist=tegra234_cbb_init).
StartOS package manifests can register plugins (e.g. Tor is a plugin service in 0.4.0) and request device grants (/dev/fuse, /dev/net/tun, /dev/kvm, hardware acceleration) as manifest flags.

Image build: rootfs is packed into a SELinux-labelled squashfs, then placed with /init into a reproducible (SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH, sorted cpio --reproducible) zstd initramfs; the OS runs from RAM, there is no separate rootfs partition

imager builds every output (iso, disk image, installer, kernel, initramfs, UKI, cmdline) from one profile: overlay first, then initramfs rebuilt with system extensions, kernel args, then a UKI signed with separate Secure Boot and PCR signers

Image Factory schematic = YAML (overlay, extraKernelArgs, META values, systemExtensions, bootloader, secureboot, disk image); schematic ID is the sha256 of its canonical form; Factory publishes a cosign public key
Image Factory core is MPL-2.0; its enterprise/ folder (SBOM, VEX, scanner, attestation, tokens) is BSL 1.1 with no Additional Use Grant, change date 2030-11-03 to MPL-2.0

Disk layout: partitions EFI, BIOS (GRUB legacy), BOOT (GRUB mode, holds A and B kernel+initramfs), META, STATE (machine config), EPHEMERAL (containerd, pods, etcd data; fills the disk), optional IMAGECACHE

Docs: upgrades use an A-B scheme retaining the previous kernel and OS image; if an upgrade fails to boot Talos rolls back; if Talos boots but workloads fail the operator must run talosctl rollback; upgrades are API-driven and scheduling is left to the user's own logic
Upgrade sequence: denyNewServices, cordon+drain, stop pods, pre-shutdown, stop containers and services, unmount, then run installer; installer writes META tag 'Upgrade' = previous boot label

Automatic revert: when the machined boot sequence returns an error, handle() calls revertBootloader, which reads the META 'Upgrade' tag and flips the bootloader default back to the previous label, then reboots; with no tag nothing is reverted
Commit point: DropUpgradeFallbackController deletes the META 'Upgrade' tag once MachineStatus is Stage=Running and Ready, once per boot

CRA (Reg. (EU) 2024/2847) applies from 2027-12-11; Article 14 (reporting) applies from 2026-09-11; Chapter IV (notified bodies) from 2026-06-11 (Art. 71(2)).

CRA Art. 13(8): support period must reflect expected use time and be at least five years (shorter only if expected use is shorter); factors include the support periods of integrated third-party components providing core functions and the availability of the operating environment.
CRA Art. 13(9): each security update made available during the support period must remain available for at least 10 years after issue or the remainder of the support period, whichever is longer.

CRA Art. 13(10): for subsequent substantially modified versions of a software product, the manufacturer may meet Annex I Part II(2) only for the latest version, provided users of earlier versions get the latest version free of charge and without extra cost to adjust their hardware/software environment.
CRA Art. 13(19): the end date of the support period (at least month and year) must be clearly specified at the time of purchase; where feasible users are notified when support ends.
CRA Art. 13(23): a manufacturer that ceases operations must inform market surveillance authorities and, as far as possible, users before cessation takes effect.

CRA Art. 14(1)-(2),(8): actively exploited vulnerabilities must be notified via the ENISA single reporting platform: early warning within 24 h, vulnerability notification within 72 h, final report within 14 days after a fix is available; impacted users must be informed.

CRA Annex I Part I(2)(c): products must ensure vulnerabilities can be addressed through security updates, including, where applicable, automatic security updates enabled as a default setting with a clear and easy opt-out, notification of updates, and the option to temporarily postpone them.

CRA Annex I Part I(2): secure-by-default configuration including reset to original state (b); confidentiality incl. encryption at rest/in transit (e); integrity (f); attack-surface limitation (j); logging with opt-out (l); secure permanent removal of all data and settings (m).

CRA Annex I Part II: SBOM in a commonly used machine-readable format covering at least top-level dependencies (1); security updates separate from functionality updates where technically feasible (2); coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy (5); security updates free of charge with advisories (8).

CRA Annex III lists 'Operating systems' (Class I, item 11), 'Boot managers' (I-8), VPN products (I-5), routers (I-12), identity management systems (I-1) and smart home general purpose virtual assistants (I-16); Class II includes 'Hypervisors and container runtime systems'.

CRA Art. 32(2): a Class I important product whose manufacturer has not applied (or only partly applied) harmonised standards, common specifications or an EU certification scheme must use EU-type examination (module B+C) or full quality assurance (module H), i.e. a notified body.

CRA Art. 32(5): manufacturers of products qualifying as free and open-source software in Annex III categories may use any Art. 32(1) procedure, including internal control (module A), provided the technical documentation is made public when the product is placed on the market.

CRA Art. 3: 'manufacturer' covers products marketed under its name whether for payment, monetisation or free of charge; an 'open-source software steward' is a legal person other than a manufacturer; recital 15 says intention to monetise, e.g. via a platform through which other services are monetised, indicates commercial activity.
CRA Art. 21-22: an importer or distributor placing a product under its own name/trademark, or anyone carrying out a substantial modification and making it available, is treated as a manufacturer.
CRA Art. 69(2)-(3): products placed on the market before 2027-12-11 are subject only if substantially modified afterwards, but Art. 14 reporting applies to all in-scope products regardless.

Raspberry Pi secure boot: boot ROM verifies against a hash of the customer RSA-2048 public key in OTP; on BCM2712 the customer key also signs the EEPROM bootloader; the bootloader verifies boot.img with boot.sig; an OTP device-unique secret unlocks a LUKS root (AES-XTS on BCM2712).

Raspberry Pi bootloader: if secure-boot is enabled, tryboot loads tryboot.img instead of boot.img, and tryboot_a_b is implicitly set when loading files from within a boot.img ramdisk (partition-level A/B).

Raspberry Pi docs: 'Raspberry Pi computers do not have a hardware protected key store'; rpi-sb-provisioner: generating the BCM2712 device key 'writes to OTP permanently and cannot be undone'; JTAG lock and signing-key programming are irreversible.

Jetson Orin secure boot (r36.4.4): the OEM generates PKC/SBK keys; fuse burning is irreversible; three PKC keys can be fused and the first two revoked; RSA-3K and ECDSA P-256/P-521 (RSA-2048 unsupported on Orin); UEFI Secure Boot enabled at flash cannot be disabled without reflashing; A/B kernel images must be signed with the db key.

Jetson Orin disk encryption (r36.4.4): LUKS AES-XTS-256; the OP-TEE luks-srv TA derives a per-device passphrase from the EKB disk-encryption key, ECID and disk UUID; mass-flashed generic keys are replaced per device at first boot.

Jetson Orin firmware TPM (r36.4.4): TPM 2.0 reference implementation as an OP-TEE TA with measured boot into PCRs; needs fused KDK0 and offline EK-certificate provisioning; online provisioning not yet available.

MCP versioning page: 'The current protocol version is 2026-07-28'; 2025-11-25 and earlier are the handshake-based revisions.

MCP 2026-07-28 removes protocol-level sessions (Mcp-Session-Id) and the initialize handshake; every request carries version and capabilities in _meta; servers MUST implement server/discover; tasks move to the extension io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks; Multi Round-Trip Requests replace server-initiated requests (roots, sampling, elicitation); SSE resumability removed.

MCP 2026-07-28 deprecates Roots, Sampling and Logging and deprecates OAuth Dynamic Client Registration; it documents OpenTelemetry trace context (traceparent, tracestate, baggage) in _meta (SEP-414) and asks servers to return tools/list in a deterministic order.

MCP 2026-07-28 authorization: MCP servers MUST implement RFC 9728 Protected Resource Metadata; MCP clients MUST implement RFC 8707 resource indicators using the server's canonical URI; servers MUST validate that tokens were issued for them as audience; authorization servers and clients SHOULD support Client ID Metadata Documents.

MCP elicitation: servers MUST NOT use form mode to request passwords, API keys, access tokens or payment credentials and MUST use URL mode for them; URL mode (introduced 2025-11-25) sends the user to an external URL so the interaction does not pass through the MCP client.

The official MCP Registry is in preview ('breaking changes or data resets may occur'), does not support private servers, and its codebase is not designed for self-hosting; private registries may implement its API to benefit from host support.

MCP extensions status table: OAuth Client Credentials Stable; Enterprise-Managed Authorization Stable; MCP Apps (interactive UI) Stable; MCP Tasks 'Beta, to Core'; Skills over MCP Beta; Server Cards Beta.
MCP governance: contributions are Apache-2.0; Lead Maintainers (BDFL) hold final decision authority; membership is for individuals, not companies.

claim: GDPR Art. 4(14) defines biometric data (e.g. facial images, dactyloscopic data) and Art. 9(1) prohibits processing biometric data 'for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person' unless an Art. 9(2) exception applies (e.g. explicit consent).

GDPR Art. 2(2)(c) excludes processing 'by a natural person in the course of a purely personal or household activity'; Recital 18 adds that the Regulation 'applies to controllers or processors which provide the means for processing personal data for such personal or household activities'.

COPPA Rule 16 CFR 312.2, as amended at 90 FR 16977 (2025-04-22): 'personal information' includes 'a biometric identifier that can be used for the automated or semi-automated recognition of an individual, such as fingerprints; ... voiceprints; gait patterns; facial templates; or faceprints'.

Washington RCW 19.375.020: a person may not enroll a biometric identifier in a database for a commercial purpose without notice, consent, or a mechanism to prevent later commercial use; 'enroll' means capture, convert to a template and store it matched to an individual.

EU AI Act Art. 2(10): the Regulation 'does not apply to obligations of deployers who are natural persons using AI systems in the course of a purely personal non-professional activity'; Art. 5(1) prohibits untargeted scraping of facial images to build recognition databases and biometric categorisation inferring race, politics, religion, sex life or orientation (Chapters I-II apply from 2 February 2025).

EU AI Act Annex III point 1 lists as high-risk: remote biometric identification (excluding verification 'the sole purpose of which is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be'), biometric categorisation by sensitive attributes, and emotion recognition.

Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of 8 July 2026 (Digital Omnibus on AI) moves the application of Chapter III Sections 1-3 to 2 December 2027 for Annex III high-risk systems and to 2 August 2028 for Annex I systems; it enters into force on the third day after publication.
